data.title: Judge opens East Potomac Park probe into potential DOJ misconduct
data.description:
A federal judge has opened an investigation into concerns that the Trump administration lied to her in the ongoing legal battle over President Trump’s desire to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links.

Friday’s hearing became the latest fiery courtroom clash between U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes and the Justice Department (DOJ), which repeatedly took issue with the judge’s lines of questioning and pushed back on any suggestion that information was wrongly withheld.

“The court will open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and DOJ attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules,” the judge said.

A preservationist group and local golfers are suing to stop major redevelopments at East Potomac Park, the longtime home of a public golf course along the edge of the nation’s capital. Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire to redevelop it into a championship-style course, and in recent days, he has said the site will close beginning Nov. 15 so the project can proceed.

The president’s comments — and recent work to cut down hundreds of trees — have escalated the legal fight.

In a flurry of recent hearings in Reyes’s courtroom, the Biden-appointed judge has repeatedly torn into DOJ attorneys about their representations on the status of the project, suggesting they were telling her something different and to not believe the president.

Reyes began on Friday by reminding the DOJ’s No. 3 official, Stanley Woodward, about professional ethics rules he is bound to follow as an attorney practicing before the court. As they continued to spar, the judge at one point told Woodward to “finish that thought internally” and to “talk about it at drinks with your friends.”

“We’re not on TV. I’m not a pundit,” Woodward pushed back at another point, also suggesting some of the judge’s questioning was blocked under executive privilege.

The judge announced she was opening the investigation after learning that the government has been working to submit the redesign plan to the National Capital Planning Commission, which examines major government projects in the Washington, D.C., area. Reyes expressed frustration that DOJ hadn’t previously told her about it. She said she’ll conduct the investigation herself or appoint a special master to do so.

As of now, the judge has restricted further tree-clearing at the golf course and has implemented new notice requirements, but she hasn’t yet outright blocked the planned closure.

“Trust but verify….no longer,” Reyes warned the government.

data.title: Education Department posts doctored image showing its HQ as Spirit Halloween
data.description:
The Education Department on Friday posted a doctored image on X showing the agency’s headquarters in Washington, D.C., with a “Spirit Halloween” banner on the building.

“These things are just popping up everywhere!” the department said in its post.

The image, posted the day before Halloween, comes as President Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon work toward a goal of closing the agency entirely.

The Education Department has made over a dozen deals with other federal agencies to outsource its responsibilities, such as moving the student loan portfolio to the Treasury Department. It has also fired thousands of employees. 

The post was faced with pushback from opponents who believe the recent moves will have a negative effect on schools and students.  

“I get asked by reporters all of the time, “Why don’t student loan borrowers trust the guidence from the federal government in repaying their loans?” Daniel Collier, an expert in higher education, posted on BlueSky. 

“From now on, I am just going to email them this post,” he added, referring to the Education Department’s image 

The Nevada State Education Association said that the department “used to play a critical role in ensuring that students with specific needs were protected, fed, and adequately supported. The dismantling, supported by Trump, McMahon, and [GOP Gov. Joe] Lombardo, will hurt Nevadans.” 

The Hill has reached out to the Education Department for comment.

data.title: ICE agent indicted in Texas after striking immigrant with vehicle
data.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who hit and injured a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas, was indicted by a grand jury in Harris County on Friday.

The 33-year-old officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was indicted on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly driving his vehicle into Miguel Parra Hernandez earlier this month, NBC News reported.

“The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said in a news conference on Friday, according to NBC.

“An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone,” Teare said.

Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old immigrant without legal status, was driving to work when federal authorities attempted to pull him over. He stopped his car, and he and his passenger attempted to run away.

Surveillance footage from the incident shows the two men running away while an SUV veers and hits Parra Hernandez, who suffered multiple injuries to his leg.

An ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to NBC that the indictment “is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians.” The spokesperson said that only federal agencies can investigate “federal officers acting in the course of their duties.”

At the press conference, Teare said that is “false.”

Following the incident, ICE said that officers observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. An immigration advocacy group, FIEL Houston, said the alleged suspect died years ago based on documentation provided by the man’s family, The New York Times reported.

In an earlier statement to The Hill, an ICE spokesperson said the claims that a federal officer purposefully hit Parra Hernandez are “RECKLESS and FALSE.”

data.title: Meta settles with second plaintiff during trial over social media addiction
data.description:
Meta settled a social media addiction lawsuit with an 18-year-old plaintiff on Friday, avoiding its next bellweather trial, which began jury selection this week.

The case, filed by a woman from Mississippi dubbed “K.D.B.,” alleged her use of Instagram and Snapchat as a child worsened her mental health and contributed to her eating disorder, suicidal thoughts, depression and self-harm.

K.D.B.’s case against Meta and Snap was consolidated with another plaintiff named S.J.’s claims against the company. Their legal teams argue the platforms intentionally designed their platforms to be addictive to young users.

In settling the case, Meta will avoid sitting through another high-profile trial during which CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, were expected to testify. Both Zuckerberg and Mosseri testified in previous trials over similar claims.

The trial will still move forward next week against Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, the plaintiffs’ attorneys confirmed.

Like K.D.B., S..J. is a teenager from Illinois who said she started using Snapchat at a young age, accessing features like “Snapstreaks” and “Snapscore” along with filters and push notifications.

Her suit alleges the features played a role in her compulsive use of Snapchat and contributed to her depression, eating disorder, anxiety and harm.

S.J. also settled her claims with Meta last week.

Emily Jeffcott, a Morgan & Morgan attorney representing K.D.B., said in a statement Friday the team remains “committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client.”

A spokesperson for Meta said “trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellweather process, and this litigation is no exception.”

Jury selection began this week and continued Friday. Jury selection is expected to continue Monday and Tuesday, followed by opening arguments the next day. Snap CEO Evan Spiegel is expected to testify, which will mark his first trial testimony.

Snap did not comment on the settlement news Friday.

Ahead of the trial’s start earlier this week,  a Snapchat spokesperson said the company was “built differently” from traditional social media platforms, arguing the claims “fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences” on the platform. 

Snapchat “opens to a camera, not a feed, not a ranking of what other people post or other social comparison metrics,” the spokesperson said. “We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources, and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first.” 

In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement for similar claims, ending a high-profile trial that was already underway in California. The settlement involved 47 U.S. states, three territories and the District of Columbia after Meta said it approached “nearly every state” to collaborate on a safety framework.  

Meta also agreed to pay Texas more than $1 billion over similar allegations.

Along with the payments, the company also agreed to set default daily time limits of two hours for users younger than 18 that can only be lifted by a parent, and it introduced blocks during the nighttime and blocked notifications during school hours. 

Meta’s spokesperson touted this agreement in a statement Friday.

“We’ve spent more than a decade building protections for teens,” the spokesperson said, adding “We hope the rest of our industry joins us in setting this new standard.”

data.title: Watch live: Trump officials announce new anti-fraud measures in Minnesota
data.description:
Top Trump administration officials are set to announce new anti-fraud measures Friday in Minnesota as the White House steps up its crackdown on fraud involving federal assistance and healthcare programs.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson will join Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald for the announcement in St. Cloud, Minn.

On Thursday, the FBI announced 168 arrests stemming from a months-long operation targeting violent crime on tribal lands across three states.

The press conference is scheduled to begin at 2 p.m. EDT.

Watch live above.

data.title: Where does push to end daylight saving time stand in Congress?
data.description:
(NewsNation) — It’s that time of year again.

As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice.

Supporters argue ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.

Where the effort to make daylight saving time permanent stands in Congress

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent daylight saving time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.

Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump’s ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to “GET IT DONE!” But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard.

Several other Republicans, particularly those from some northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it.

“You’d be sending kids to school in the dark,” said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds.

Despite pressure from Trump, several Republicans predicted in recent weeks the bill won’t come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election.

Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said it’s his understanding that the House bill is a “nonstarter” for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon.

“No way,” Moreno said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn’t weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

data.title: Hold the rate. The Fed can't pump oil.
data.description:
At its recent meeting, the Federal Reserve decided to maintain its interest rate target, forgoing a hike that would have been the second in six weeks. The target federal funds rate remained between 3.75 percent and 4 percent, with two members of the Federal Open Market Committee dissenting.

The Fed should be commended for its decision. While some may argue that recent inflation justified a rate hike, the increase in aggregate prices was almost entirely predicated on energy cost increases. The fact is that no central bank on earth has ever lowered the price of a barrel of crude by raising the cost of a home equity line of credit.

Consumer prices are up 3.7 percent over the past year. Energy is up 20 percent and gasoline 34 percent. Energy alone accounts for about 1.4 points of that 3.7 — around the same as housing, which normally drives the index and carries more than a third of its weight. When the energy shock is stripped out, the inflation picture changes dramatically.

Economists, and indeed the Fed, know that energy is the most volatile component, which is why they point to core inflation, the index that leaves out food and energy prices. However, even that might not provide the full picture of just how much oil price changes permeate the entire economy.

The issue is that core removes prices by category, not by what drives them. Despite jet fuel being one of the highest costs an airline pays, airline fares are counted within core; fares are up 22 percent over the year. So are the trucking and delivery charges baked into the price of nearly everything in shopping malls.

Reaching a better methodology would require asking this: What would inflation have been if energy and the goods and services that are most energy intensive had risen at a normal 2 percent rate while measuring the realized prices of everything else?

Using the Labor Department’s own weights for the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the answer is 2.1 percent over the past year and about 2.5 percent over the past three months. Month by month, even as crude oil rose from the low $80s to above $100, this measure was 0.20, 0.22, and 0.21 percent, respectively.

If we apply the same methodology to the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the Fed’s preferred method of measuring inflation, that figure is still at 2.6 percent year over year. This includes the latest September Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index data that was released on Oct. 29, the day after the Fed meeting, further reinforcing that the Fed made the right choice.

The Fed’s own regional banks also reach the same conclusion through a different calculation. The Dallas Fed’s “trimmed mean” measure, which discards the largest price swings each month, fell to 2.2 percent in August, its lowest reading of the year. The Cleveland Fed’s median price index was at 2.6 percent in September. Every one of these methods says that inflation is within a point of the target.

In August, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh argued at Jackson Hole that inflation is “widespread” because more than half of the 199 categories in the government’s price index rose faster than 3 percent. The problem with this framing is that it equally weighs all goods categories, regardless of how much of a family’s budget each constitutes.

The above measures show that when one accounts for what portion of household budgets go to various items, inflation is not widespread; it is instead largely limited to oil-dependent items. In these circumstances, there was little justification to reach for a blunt instrument whose costs fall on the entire economy.

An October hike would have put unwarranted pressure on Americans. Families would have faced higher payments on car loans and credit cards. Small businesses would have paid more to borrow. Not to mention the fact that the effects of an interest rate change take a year or more to fully suffuse through the economy, meaning the full effects of a hike would have persisted far longer than the current energy shock.

The Fed was right to hold rates in October, and moving forward, they should also give greater weight to measures that account for the kind of narrow price shocks that we see today. Whether it’s the “trimmed mean” or holding energy-intensive goods to 2 percent, the public deserves to know what specifically is driving price changes, which in turn also provides them with greater clarity on long-run trends.

Warsh also indicated that some future meetings would focus on monetary policy strategy, not just rate setting. This bodes well for taking seriously the reports from the taskforces he created upon taking office, particularly the two looking at improving the data the Fed uses to make policy and the appropriate size of the Fed’s balance sheet.

Interest rates are a powerful lever but must be targeted towards inflation pressures that are responsive to interest rate changes. Higher rates do not correct for an energy shock derived from a war in the Middle East.

Michael Faulkender is co-chair, Economy and Trade Policy; chair, AI and Emerging Technology Policy at AFPI and former deputy secretary of the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Jeff Schlagenhauf is director of Economy and Trade Policy at AFPI.

data.title: Charlamagne rips Nicki Minaj for bashing Kathy Hochul, but not Trump
data.description:
Charlamagne tha God is calling out Nicki Minaj, and his argument isn’t simply about her political support for New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman. It’s about whether the moral standards she demands of others are standards she’s willing to apply to the politicians she supports.  

Here’s the backstory. On Wednesday, Minaj took aim at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, posting a series of tweets questioning her character and religious standing.  

She wrote, “Kathy Hochul is an evil woman. The Democratic Party should forfeit her seat because even if she wins, she will be of great consequence to them. Downward spiral for her. She will not escape God’s wrath.”  

Minaj also challenged Christians who would vote for Hochul saying how dare they.   

Where is that same religious indignation when it comes to President Trump? His record includes serial infidelity, derogatory remarks about women, racially charged rhetoric about immigrants and Muslim Americans, and a civil jury finding him liable for sexually abusing E. Jean Carroll. He also declared, “I HATE MY OPPONENT” at a funeral.  

But I’ll let Charlemagne break it down:  

“Listen, Nicki’s words, her statement — it just lacks moral consistency. That’s selective outrage, if you ask me. Because you can have whatever political belief you want, but you need to hold everybody to the same moral standard, Nicki.” 

He continues: “Like, you support Donald Trump. And you can support Trump — that’s your thing. If you want to support him, support him. But when you start using words like ‘evil’ and telling people God is going to punish them, accusing other people of failing to condemn wrongdoing, now I start to look at you crazy, because do you know who you are even supporting?”  

“I don’t want to hear nothing about morals when it comes to Donald Trump,” said Charlemagne. “You can’t condemn nobody’s morality when you support a person who is like Donald Trump. Who has had more moral controversies than Donald Trump?!”  

Oh I forgot to mention how Trump was recently talking about Minaj. Take a look:  

“By the way I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before, Nicki Minaj,” said the president. “That’s hard to miss!”  

Is that the standard of respect and character we want to normalize? And why does moral accountability seem to become less important when the person being scrutinized belongs to your political team?  

Policy is a whole other issue here. Politico reports that Blakeman, who wants to replace Hochul as governor, still had no policy section on his campaign website. Instead of offering detailed proposals, he has largely focused on attacking the incumbent. When asked in August about reining in housing costs, for example, a major concern for New Yorkers, Blakeman pivoted and said “It’s not through socialism.”  

I’m down to be critical of Hochul — she should face scrutiny, and Minaj has every right to criticize her. But if the core argument is about morality, Christians and divine punishment, then the standard has to be consistent.  

Nicki Minaj is entitled to her politics, but moral authority requires more than condemning the people you oppose. I’m going to need her to explain why the same scrutiny doesn’t apply to the people she adamantly supports.  

 Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

data.title: GOP House member on 'embarrassing' SC prospects: 'Darline is dragging Rs'
data.description:
A House Republican called the competitive Senate race in South Carolina “embarrassing,” adding that incumbent Sen. Darline Graham (R) is “dragging Rs down the ticket.”

“Republicans won this seat by 18 points. The fact it’s this close and the speaker has to come to SC 1 to drag the R across the finish line is embarrassing,” the anonymous member wrote in an exchange posted Thursday by NewsNation senior congressional correspondent Joe Khalil on the social platform X.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is expected to campaign in South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, according to local news station WCSC.

A tight Senate race is unfolding in South Carolina between Graham and her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) leans in favor of Graham, giving her a 65 percent chance of winning the race.

However, a recent a New York Times/Siena University poll showed both candidates with 48 percent support among likely voters in South Carolina, a state which has not elected a Democrat to the upper chamber of Congress since 1998.

“Darline is dragging Rs down the ticket” the Republican member wrote, as recounted in Khalil’s post. “The only saving grace is that the governors race is where it should be.”

President Trump recently made his third and final trip to South Carolina to boost support for Graham’s Senate bid. Graham was appointed to the seat by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R).

In the state’s gubernatorial race, South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson (R) has a 74 percent chance of winning against his Democratic opponent Jermaine Johnson, according to DDHQ.
